title: EFFECTS OF INTERIOR COLOR SCHEMES ON EMOTION, TASK PERFORMANCE, AND HEART RATE IN IMMERSIVE VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENTS
research_question: To investigate the effects of interior color schemes in immersive virtual environments (IVEs) on emotion, task performance, and heart rate to examine IVEs' potential for interior color research.

participants.description: Student participants (7 females, 48 males), Asian, 20-28 years old (M = 21.34, SD = 1.44), from Hong Kong Polytechnic University. 49 were engineering students, rest from other majors.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through flyers on campus, given a gift coupon for participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four different colored immersive virtual environment (IVE) models (red, green, blue, and white) of an interior space. Wall colors were structured differently while other parameters (lighting level at 500 lx, indoor temperature at 23°C, real-life objects like carpeting, acoustical ceiling tile, texture, and doors) remained constant. Colors chosen based on Kwallek et al. (1996) as 6.05R 4.59/11.15 (red), 9.75YR 8.74/0.45 (white), 3.45G 4.44/7.89 (green), and 2.43 PB 5.12/10.51 (blue).

measures.instrument: Questionnaire with eight bipolar adjective pairs (Heavy/Light, Calm/Exciting, Weak/Strong, Cool/Warm, Tense/Relax, Unpleasant/Pleasant, Interesting/Boring, Dark/Light) on a 1-7 semantic scale, selected from the Color Image Scale (Kobayashi, 1981).
Proofreading exercise (number of errors per minute, ENPM).
Polar H7 real-time heart rate sensor (measured during normal conditions as baseline and during experimental session).
Simplified Igroup Presence Questionnaire (IPQ) with five questions on a 5-point Likert scale (1=strongly disagree, 5=strongly agree), focusing on 'sense of being physically present'.

mechanisms: Color symbolism and psychological associations: Different colors evoke distinct emotional responses based on cultural and individual experiences.
Arousal modulation: Color schemes can influence physiological arousal, which in turn affects cognitive performance (Yerkes-Dodson law).

Sense of presence in IVEs: Immersive virtual environments with one-to-one scale modeling, 3D visualization, and isolation from the surrounding environment promote a strong sense of 'being there', enhancing ecological validity.
Cognitive resource modulation: Environmental features, including color, can affect the allocation of cognitive resources, influencing task performance.
moderators: Exposure time to color schemes (discussed as a potential factor for heart rate changes)
Individual differences in participants' ability to screen out irrelevant stimuli (discussed for task performance)
Age and gender (mentioned as factors affecting color perception in literature review and limitations)
Cultural and geographical proximity (mentioned as factors affecting color perception in literature review and limitations)
implementation_implications: IVEs have potential for interior color research to overcome limitations of traditional tools, offering better controllability and cost-effectiveness.
Interior designers could use IVEs to quickly test user responses to various color schemes for their projects, potentially leading to higher user satisfaction.
Calming color schemes (blue, white, green) can reduce heart rate, suggesting their use in environments where stress reduction is desired.
White color schemes may enhance task performance for simple tasks like proofreading.

tables.description: IVE Igroup Presence Questionnaire results on sense of presence
key_stats: Mean (SD) for 5 questions: 3.56 (1.01) to 3.82 (0.77) for presence, 3.17 (0.98) for perceiving pictures.

limitations: Wearing an HMD can cause discomfort or dizziness, making IVEs unsuitable for studies requiring longer observation periods or specific participant behaviors.
Participants might have been conscious of researchers observing them, potentially leading to a Hawthorn effect.
Three IVE environments used highly saturated colors that may not reflect real-world interior spaces, limiting generalizability.
The study involved only local college students, limiting generalizability to other populations (e.g., employees, older adults).
Nearsighted participants perceived IVE models as blurry through the HMD, potentially decreasing sense of presence and precise color perception.

Only emotion, heart rate, and proofreading performance were used as indicators of user experience, limiting generalizability to other indicators (e.g., environmental satisfaction, cognitive performance).
All participants were Asian, and human perception of color can vary by culture and geographical proximity.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of Interior Color Schemes on Emotion, Task Performance, and Heart Rate in Immersive Virtual Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of Interior Color Schemes on Emotion, Task Performance, and Heart Rate in Immersive Virtual Environments
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the effects of interior color schemes in immersive virtual environments (IVEs) on emotion, task performance, and heart rate to examine IVEs’ potential for interior color research. Fifty–five ( n = 55) student participants were recruited to experience four different colored IVE models (i.e., red, green, blue, and white), and their emotions, heart rate change, and proofreading performances during the immersion were measured. Participants were also asked about their sense of presence after the experience. The findings support the following three hypotheses: (1) IVE interior color schemes affect subject emotion, (2) IVE interior color schemes affect subject task performance as measured through a proofreading exercise, and (3) IVE interior color schemes affect subject heart rate. Specifically, red was perceived as significantly heavier, warmer, more exciting, tenser, and unpleasant. Significantly fewer errors occurred during the white immersion versus the green color scheme when completing the task performance exercise. While heart rate was reduced for each color, significant decreases were detected in the blue, white, and green color scenarios. The majority of participants felt a sense of being there when experiencing the four colored IVE spaces. Based on these results, we conclude that IVE has potential for interior color research to overcome the limitations of traditional color research tools.
